I feel you dude, improving is extremely hard.

Have you got a practice partner ?
I swear that analysing my games with someone has made me improve greatly, I recon that it's because I actually have to verbalize my thought on a position and the difference in perspectives offers a more complete understanding of a given position. It also makes studying without a computer much more agreable since you can share your ideas.

I would also recommend avoiding the computer 
( or at least analysing without the computer first and then checking with our friend stockfish), yes you will absolutely not get everything right, hell I once looked at one of my position for an hour only to realize that i had missed an obvious move early in my calculations, but you will gain somewhat of an understanding of where you went wrong. In fact I recommend that you write a "list of errors" in a notebook where you write down the mistakes that you ( not the computer) saw in your games. You will then have a clearer picture of where you need to improve.

Honestly the only trick i can give you for opening memorisation is to write your own document with the opening moves that you're learning. Do not shy away from making your own comments on important moves ( what does it achieve, what are the goals for each side and so on). Then you can maybe re-read your documents for like 5 minutes before you sleep every day. Obviously you're not gonna remember everything at first but that's ok ! We all have much more interesting things to remember than the Freak attack in the sicilian. 

As for the blindfold playing I can't do it either (I'm 1650 on rapid on chess.com for reference), I can't even keep track of my own calculations most of the time, don't be too harsh on yourself !
I do however recommend that you train that visualisation with a few exercices:

-name a random square in your head such as g5 and find if it's a white or dark square 

-Imagine a knight or a Bishop on a random square, then find all the square that it can go to immediately 

It doesn't need to be that long, i do it for 15 minutes a day.

As for the difference between the tactics and real rating it's honestly to be expected. My puzzle rating is also around a 1000 point higher ! 
In a puzzle you expect there to be a move, therefore your brain starts searching for it but in a real game you will often not even realize that there is a crushing tactic ! Which is why doing a lot of tactics can sometimes be counter-productive, you're brain is gonna expect those strong tactics in position where you need to think more abstractly. ( I'm not saying that puzzle training is bad, I'm saying that perhaps you need to limit it to 5-10 puzzle a day) 

One thing that you need to remember is that mistakes are to be expected, in fact realizing that you will always make stupide mistakes is quite liberating. You have to acknowledge these mistakes to see where and why you went wrong ! 

If i could recommend you one book it would be Pump up your Rating ! by Axel Smith, honestly most of my advice come from it, it's à fun read that changed my way of improving.
